hints: Look at W in Fig. 6.1 and compare it with $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. Which two $\text{OH}$ groups have been replaced, and by what atom?
walkthrough:
Spot the two functional groups that change**
Look closely at $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH}$. It has an alcohol $\text{OH}$ and a carboxylic acid $\text{OH}$. In W, $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COCl}$, both $\text{OH}$ groups have become $\text{Cl}$. Remember $\text{SOCl}_2$ replaces any $\text{OH}$ attached to carbon with $\text{Cl}$.

Balance with excess reagent**
Because two $\text{OH}$ groups react, you need $2\text{SOCl}_2$. Each gives $\text{SO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ as by products, so the balanced equation is $\text{HOCH}_2\text{COOH} + 2\text{SOCl}_2 \rightarrow \text{ClCH}_2\text{COCl} + 2\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$.

hints: Think about what acidic species are present after W reacts with the amine X to form the amide Y.
walkthrough:
Remember acid is always made when an acyl chloride reacts**
When $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COCl}$ reacts with $\text{ArNH}_2$, the $\text{Cl}$ from the $\text{COCl}$ group leaves as $\text{HCl}$. That $\text{HCl}$ would protonate unreacted amine or product. Adding $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa(aq)}$, a base, neutralises this acid and any unreacted acidic W.
Final answer: To neutralise / remove excess $\text{H}^+$ / acid produced, such as $\text{HCl}$, or any unreacted acidic W.

hints: Start by identifying the nucleophile in $\text{ArNH}_2$ and the electrophilic carbon in $\text{ClCH}_2\text{COCl}$.
Recall the two stages of addition-elimination at an acyl chloride: addition to form a tetrahedral intermediate, then reformation of C=O with loss of Cl-.
Remember to show the $\delta+$ on C and $\delta-$ on O, and to draw the arrow from the C=O bond to O in the addition step.
Think about what the negative oxygen does in the elimination step and where the C-Cl bonding electrons must go.
walkthrough:
Set up the attack**
Picture $\text{ArNH}_2$ meeting $\text{ClCH}_2\text{C(=O)Cl}$. The nitrogen has a lone pair, so it is the nucleophile. The carbonyl carbon is $\delta+$ because oxygen pulls electrons away, so mark $\text{C}^{\delta+}\text{=O}^{\delta-}$. Draw a curly arrow from the N lone pair to the $\text{C}^{\delta+}$.

Form the tetrahedral intermediate**
As N bonds to C, the $\text{C=O}$ cannot keep both bonds. Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C=O}$ bond up to O. This gives a tetrahedral intermediate with $\text{O}^-$, $\text{Cl}$, $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and $\text{NH}_2^+\text{Ar}$ all on the same carbon. Charges must be shown.

Collapse back to the carbonyl**
Now the $\text{O}^-$ lone pair pushes back down. Draw a curly arrow from $\text{O}^-$ to reform $\text{C=O}$. This pushes out the best leaving group.

Expel chloride**
Draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-Cl}$ bond to $\text{Cl}$ to give $\text{Cl}^-$. You now have the amide $\text{ClCH}_2\text{CONHAr}$ (Y) after loss of $\text{H}^+$. That addition then elimination sequence is the key pattern for all acyl chlorides.

Final answer: Addition: lone pair on $\text{ArNH}_2$ attacks $\delta+ \text{C=O}$; $\text{C=O}$ bond breaks to $\text{O}^{\delta-}$ to give tetrahedral intermediate $\text{ClCH}_2\text{C(O}^-\text{)(Cl)(NH}_2^+\text{Ar)}$. Elimination: lone pair on $\text{O}^-$ reforms $\text{C=O}$; $\text{C-Cl}$ bond breaks to $\text{Cl}^-$. Correct dipoles and curly arrows shown.

hints: Recall the definition of a nucleophile in terms of electrons, then look for that feature on the N atom in $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}$.
walkthrough:
Link structure to nucleophile behaviour**
A nucleophile is an electron pair donor. In $(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5)_2\text{NH}$ the nitrogen has a lone pair that is not used in bonding. It can donate this pair to the $\delta+$ carbon of the $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ group in Y in reaction 2.
Final answer: Nitrogen has a lone pair / pair of electrons that it can donate to an electron deficient carbon.

hints: In TLC, remember which phase moves up the plate by capillary action and which phase stays fixed as a solid coating.
walkthrough:
Separate moving from fixed**
The solvent, here ethyl ethanoate, flows up the plate, so it is the mobile phase. The solid coating that does not move, silica ($\text{SiO}_2$) or alumina ($\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$), is the stationary phase that adsorbs the compounds.
Final answer: mobile phase = ethyl ethanoate; stationary phase = silica / $\text{SiO}_2$ or alumina / $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$.

hints: Think about the two distances you measure from the baseline on a developed TLC plate.
walkthrough:
State the ratio**
Measure from the origin line to the centre of the spot, and from the origin line to the solvent front. Then $R_f$ = distance moved by solute divided by distance moved by solvent front. It has no units and is always less than 1.
Final answer: $R_f$ = distance travelled by solute / compound / spot $\div$ distance travelled by solvent front.

hints: A smaller $R_f$ means the compound spent more time stuck and less time moving, so compare attraction to the stationary phase versus solubility in the mobile phase.
walkthrough:
Interpret the lower Rf**
$R_f$ for X is 0.49 versus 0.71 for lidocaine, so X moves less far. That means X sticks more strongly to the polar silica stationary phase, while lidocaine spends more time dissolved in the ethyl ethanoate mobile phase and is carried further.
Final answer: X is more strongly adsorbed / has greater affinity for the stationary phase than lidocaine, or lidocaine is more soluble in the mobile phase solvent.

hints: Look at the $\text{N(CH}_2\text{CH}_3)_2$ part of lidocaine and apply the n+1 rule to the $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{CH}_3$ and vice versa.
walkthrough:
Recognise the classic ethyl pattern**
The signals at $\delta$ 2.6 and $\delta$ 1.1 come from the two equivalent $\text{NCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ groups. The $\text{CH}_2$ sees 3 H on the neighbouring $\text{CH}_3$, so n+1 = 4, a quartet. The $\text{CH}_3$ sees 2 H on the neighbouring $\text{CH}_2$, so n+1 = 3, a triplet.
Final answer: $\delta$ 2.6 = quartet; $\delta$ 1.1 = triplet.

hints: Use Table 6.2 to match $\delta$ 7.1, 3.0 and 2.3 to proton environments, noting that aromatic H appears above 6.0 ppm.
For the two signals with 1:3 integration, think which group in lidocaine has 2H next to C=O and which has 6H from two identical methyls on the ring.
walkthrough:
Assign the aromatic signal**
$\delta$ 7.1 falls in the 6.0 to 9.0 ppm range for $\text{H-Ar}$. Lidocaine has three aromatic protons on the disubstituted ring, so this fits perfectly.

Use integration to separate the alkyl signals**
The ratio $\delta$ 3.0 : $\delta$ 2.3 is 1:3. The $\text{COCH}_2\text{N}$ group has 2H and appears at 2.2 to 3.0 ppm for alkyl next to $\text{C=O}$, giving the $\delta$ 3.0 singlet. The two $\text{ArCH}_3$ groups give 6H in total, three times the area, and appear at 2.3 to 3.0 ppm for alkyl next to aromatic ring, giving the $\delta$ 2.3 singlet.

Final answer: $\delta$ 7.1 = protons attached to aromatic ring / $\text{H-Ar}$; $\delta$ 3.0 = $\text{CH}_2$ next to $\text{C=O}$ / $\text{-CH}_2\text{-C=O}$; $\delta$ 2.3 = methyl groups next to aromatic ring / $\text{CH}_3\text{-Ar}$.

hints: Count carbons in lidocaine but remember that symmetry makes some carbons equivalent, especially in the $\text{N(C}_2\text{H}_5)_2$ group and the symmetric dimethylphenyl ring.
walkthrough:
Count unique carbon environments**
Draw lidocaine and look for symmetry. The two ethyl groups are identical (2 types: $\text{CH}_2$ and $\text{CH}_3$), the two ring methyls are identical (1 type), the symmetric 2,6-dimethylphenyl ring gives 4 aromatic types, plus one $\text{C=O}$ and one $\text{COCH}_2$ carbon. That totals $2 + 1 + 4 + 2 = 9$ distinct $^{13}\text{C}$ peaks.
